analysis.one_liner: Lets people erase their personal data from all data brokers with one free request through the FTC.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on April 2, 2025 and has never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and has no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The DELETE Act would make the Federal Trade Commission build a free website where anyone can file one request to delete their personal information from every registered data broker at once. Data brokers — companies that buy and sell people's personal information without ever having a direct relationship with them — would have to register with the FTC, publicly disclose what data they collect and how to opt out, check a secure registry regularly, and delete matching data within 31 days. They would face independent audits and FTC enforcement if they fail to comply.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people gain a single, free way to wipe their personal data — names, addresses, browsing history, biometric and genetic information, inferences about them — out of the hands of data brokers that currently sell it, and to stop those brokers from collecting it again. People targeted by stalkers, scammers, or identity thieves, and anyone uncomfortable with being profiled, benefit most; the request is free to individuals.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a one-stop, free FTC website where a person can demand deletion of their data from every registered data broker at once, instead of hunting down each broker individually.
Brokers must check the FTC's hashed registries at least every 31 days and delete matching records within 31 days, including data held by affiliates, and stop future collection.
Data brokers must register annually with the FTC and publicly disclose what data they collect, where it comes from, and how to opt out — in downloadable, machine-readable form.
Brokers face FTC enforcement, annual completion-rate reports, and independent third-party audits every three years, with violations treated as unfair or deceptive practices.

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers pay registration and system-access fees and bear the cost of deleting records, auditing themselves every three years, and rebuilding their databases. The FTC pays to build and run the system, funded by those fees and capped at 1% of expected operating cost per broker.

drawbacks.text: Data brokers would face registration, hashing queries, deletion duties, annual reporting, and third-party audits; industry would likely argue the compliance costs are significant and that a centralized deletion registry concentrates sensitive data in one government-run system.
The bill targets only data brokers — companies people deal with directly can keep collecting, and exclusions for fraud prevention and identity verification keep some data flows going.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the benefits — a free, one-stop deletion of their data from every registered broker — clearly outweigh the costs, which fall on data brokers as compliance and audit expenses and on the FTC as the cost of building the system (offset by broker fees). Privacy advocates would note it leaves collection by non-brokers (the companies consumers deal with directly) untouched, and a centralized registry of what people want deleted is itself a honeypot, though the bill mandates strong cryptographic protections. No organized opposition appears in the record.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on April 2, 2025, and nothing has happened since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: The bill's only actions are introduction and referral to committee on April 2, 2025; the Energy and Commerce Committee has taken no further action.
The bill has zero cosponsors, so no other member of the House has put their name on it.
The bill would require data brokers to register with the FTC and honor deletion requests submitted through a single free FTC-run system.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers are better off so far: the bill sits untouched in committee, so their business model continues unchanged.

against.name: Data broker industry
against.what_they_did: No organized public position appears in the record; the bill would impose registration, deletion, audit, and fee obligations on data brokers, who have historically opposed such regulation.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and the bill has no cosponsors from either party, so the partisan shape is unknown.

industries.note: The bill's whole purpose is to shrink their business: mandatory registration and public disclosure of their data practices, a one-stop deletion system that empties their databases on request, reporting, and triennial audits. Their interest here runs against consumers' ability to erase their data.
Companies that collect data with a direct customer relationship are not 'data brokers' under the bill's definition, so their first-party data practices continue largely untouched.
Consumer reporting agencies and identity-verification/fraud-prevention uses are expressly excluded from the bill, so that industry keeps operating as before.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Energy and Commerce Committee with no cosponsors and no announced action; most solo-sponsored privacy bills die in committee without a hearing, and passage is unlikely unless the committee schedules it or similar provisions are folded into a larger data privacy package.
